stories.title_en: Reading and writing are less symmetric than you (probably) think

comments.author: Pannoniae
comments.text:
Great article :D The rabbithole actually goes even deeper because buffering on the read side is almost always good, but reads are often way more latency-sensitive than writes. Which leads to the paradox that increasing the buffer size / prefetching more with mmapping can lead to worse performance due to the added latency. And decreasing the buffer size can have the same effect due to issuing more calls, so in order to squeeze in the optimal throughput/latency ratio on reads you have to tune it per workload.... or just try a few different buffer sizes and see which one works better.
Writes are the opposite, they're usually not RAW (read-after-write), they're "fire and forget", so you don't really care about latency, but you do care a whole a lot about your writes actually arriving... again two competing parameters because the more you batch the writes, the faster they are but the bigger chance of a torn write or data loss. And unlike reads, writes are
not
idempotent on the application level so ideally you'd want some logic to atomically write a meaningful amount of data so it won't get torn, even if it crashes.

I think the royal combo is Lean 4/TLA+/etc. plus AI plus a deterministic generator. For large systems formal method assertions need to be compressed down to a human comprehensible size. This can happen when the assertions are confirming the accuracy of a model and its attached code generators. The generator can generate proofs of the generated code and a human only needs to ensure that the generator provably generates the correct mass scale assertions.
This is how formal methods can constrain AI for large systems.
We're doing this at the Open Markets Initiative, where we've generated millions of lines of Lean 4, TLA+, and Rocq that ensure that our open source electronic trading protocol code is accurate. We didn't expect it but the Lean prover did identify some incorrect steps.

stories.title_en: Cisco gives engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code

comments.author: linsomniac
comments.text:
We just recently use Claude Code to port an old Coldfusion site to Java Spring and it went amazingly well.  It's around 50K lines of Java, one of our engineers did it in his spare time over about a week, using the $200/mo Claude plan.  We had been talking about doing it for at least the last dozen years but never found the time.  It would have taken around 12-18 engineer-months to do this manually.
He had the translation use browser integration to compare the new site to the old site automatically.  The result was so good that he had to change background color on the new site because he couldn't be sure that he was testing the new site; it was so close to the original he was paranoid about accidentally being on the old site and not knowing it.  The whole thing was done in under 2 weeks, including coding, developer testing, tester testing, and deployment.  It's been in production 4-6 weeks now and we've had no reports of problems.

comments.author: grey-area
comments.text:
Translating from one language/platform to another is something AI is very very good at, so this sounds like a good use of it, bonus points if they create a comprehensive test suite first.
Yes it will lead to new bugs, but the older code probably contains a ton of bugs already and is probably difficult to update (original writers long gone, docs out of date etc), so this is probably the best way out of that situation,
as long as
proper support is given afterwards so they don't end up in the same situation a year later (this is the hard bit).
The ra-ra commentary from the CEO is somewhat off-putting, but the idea is not all bad.

comments.author: Verdex
comments.text:
"Where there's no sense, there's no feeling". The words, I am told, of my father's maternal grandmother.  It is strange to feel such an intense kinship and to inhabit so closely the mind space of a woman who I have never met.
Perhaps I'm merely feeling my age.  But while I suspect Cisco will eventually be disappointed, my emotional state remains a profound void.  There is no feeling.
I reserve empathy instead towards those at Cisco who chose rightly in life.  They get to work, they do the job, they return home, they feed their family bread.  Please endure the 'vision' of your corporate masters.  You have already arrived and your destination is good.
When I was young I was told the book of Ecclesiastes was depressing.  But with age I see it as a book of hope.  Your job is pointless and that will never change regardless of your token burn rate.  Enjoy your family as the sun sets.

comments.author: gosen
comments.text: Such a risky idea to let one person rewrite the whole legacy. I mean there's a chance that this guy thinks about maintenance and how all his creations will me supported when he's done, but something tells me that he just want to show that he can do it and the rest of the tech team will be suffering. Good luck to that guy anyway

comments.author: balderdash
comments.text: We have an embedded system in one of product offerings that was largely developed using a bunch of “antiquated” technologies (over the past twenty years) and over the past year the two software devs that maintained it have retired. This normally would have big problem, but the entire codebase was re-written, documented, and modernized in a matter of about 3 months (for about $20k in tokens, and a mid level developer spending 50% of their time on it over that period). So it doesn’t surprise me to think a company like Cisco has piles of situations like this.

comments.author: RoadieRoller
comments.text:
Not something at Cisco scale. But a co-founder and I, rewrote a dating app we had written in Ionic/Angular/SpringBoot/Postgres to React-Native/NextJS/Supabase in two weeks, and released it without the users/paid subscribers not knowing what happened, but they were happy to see the new slick/faster interface.
We had developed the original app in 2020-2021 when Covid was around, and we were bored sitting at home not having much to do, and wanted to learn Angular. Our employer/company we worked for, wanted all of us to be to be Full-stack and both of us were backend developers. Hence we did our dating app as a side project as my co-founder was single.
Initially it was a $100 Claude Max license, and we were maxxing it at every stage, but once rewritten, $20 is good enough to maintain it.

comments.author: candl
comments.text: I run some Huawei networking equipment under VRP OS (switches, OLTs). CLI is almost identical to iOS, but commands have alternative naming (e.g. show -> display, but many more such instances wherever possible - often times I prefer the naming in VRP). Apparently even the first editions of VRP documentation had parts citing cisco verbatim or had references to cisco docs. Rumors say its origins are stolen iOS source code at some point in the past via corporate espionage. The irony of this is that this cisco codebase has been rewritten at least once by the chinese before LLMs ;).

comments.author: Buttons840
comments.text:
I'd feel a lot better if I knew some red team security researchers were going hard trying to break into critical national infrastructure, just to ensure it's not too easy, but probably this isn't happening because it would be a felony to even try. The bad guys are free to try though.
All this will tend to get blamed on AI, but AI didn't put these vulnerabilities into place. AI is just a tool that can be used to discover vulnerabilities, and the only question we have to answer is whether or not that tool should be available to regular people.
Some will try to frame the question as being about whether we should allow AI aid in cyber-security, but that's not the question. This technology isn't going away. The bad guys will have it. Nations will have it. Again, the question is, can regular people also continue to have it?
